title: Settle here, scatter there
hookLine: tradition says Nanak blessed a rude village to stay put and a kind one to scatter, so goodness would spread

lines: KINDNESS, AND THEN: MAY YOU SCATTER.
cards: Two travelers come into a village at dusk, dusty and hungry. Doors close as they pass. Someone laughs at their clothes.
Someone tells them to move along. Nobody offers water. In the morning, as they leave, one of them, Nanak, gives the village a blessing: may you stay here, settled, just as you are.

The other, Mardana, says nothing. A day later, a different village feeds them, gives them a place to sleep, and sends them off with bread for the road. And as they leave, the blessing is: may you be scattered.

teach.b: In the sakhi, Mardana can't hold it in. The rude village gets to stay comfortable, and the good village gets broken up? That's backward.
Tradition gives Nanak's answer, roughly: if the unkind people stay where they are, their unkindness stays with them. If the kind people scatter, their kindness goes everywhere they go.
Wherever they settle, a new village learns how to welcome a stranger. This sakhi surprises on purpose.
It sounds like a curse and a blessing swapped, and the surprise is the teaching; Mardana says out loud what a listener might be thinking. It also changes what a blessing is for.
Here, a blessing isn't a reward handed to the deserving to keep. It's a seed, and seeds are meant to be carried.
For the people scattered, leaving home is hard, and the story doesn't pretend it isn't. It says even a hard move can carry something good into a new place. And the rude village?
Nanak doesn't curse it. He leaves it in peace, as it is. The story isn't about punishing anyone.
It's about where goodness goes: a meal, a place to sleep, bread for the road, carried out of one village and set down in many.

how: Sikhs tell this sakhi of the two villages to explain that goodness is meant to travel.

o: a command to the kind village to stay home
a curse Nanak put on the village that fed him
the blessing Nanak gave the unkind village

games.q: inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a seed meant to be carried

s: in the sakhi, Nanak curses the rude village
he blesses it to stay as it is; nobody is cursed.
he said it sounded backward, and Nanak explained.
the kind village was scattered as a punishment
it was scattered so its kindness would spread wherever its people went.

games.q: you're Mardana. Nanak has just blessed the kind village to scatter and the rude one to stay. what do you do?
o: keep quiet; the Guru knows best.
ask him why; it sounds backward.
go back and warn the kind village.
games.why: in the sakhi Mardana asks, and Nanak explains: unkindness stays put, goodness travels.

practice: Think of a kindness someone showed you: a neighbor who brought food, a teacher who stayed late, a stranger who held a door in the rain.
Then picture a place you'll be today where nobody knows that kindness exists, and see it arriving there with you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath.

wordCard.voice: Settle here. The blessing Nanak gave the unkind village in the sakhi, while the kind one was blessed to scatter, so its goodness would travel.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: may you stay settled, the blessing given to the rude village in the telling.

carryVoice: Your line: goodness spreads. Kindness, scattered, travels with the people who carry it. Seven hundred forty-one days, and counting.
